1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	EC-HTE requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
5	For $K{=}2$, EC-HTE remains effective even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$ (Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}); for $K{=}4$, $P(Z{=}1) \geq 0.3$ is needed to approach breakeven with global correction at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$.
6	Even above this threshold, stratification incurs a variance cost: at $K{=}4$, extreme heterogeneity, and $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$, CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
7	The method also requires moderate baseline classifier accuracy per subgroup; when any subgroup's FNR or FPR approaches 0.5, the confusion matrix row approaches a uniform distribution and inversion amplifies noise (Appendix~\ref{app:semireal}), as confirmed independently in the hate speech case study (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
8	These failure modes interact: high per-subgroup error-rate variance combined with low minority prevalence $P(Z{=}1)$ jointly reduces effective per-subgroup expert labels for the positive class, compounding both sources of estimation error.
9	Additionally, our main semi-synthetic experiments use constant treatment effects across subgroups; a supplementary heterogeneous-$\tau$ DGP (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}) shows that EC-HTE achieves targeted bias and RMSE improvement in subgroups with large $\Delta\tau$, though aggregate RMSE remains comparable to global correction.
10	At $K{=}8$ with $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ (${\approx}31$ labels/subgroup), EC-HTE maintains nominal coverage (95.6\%) but RMSE exceeds global correction, establishing $K{=}8$ as a scalability boundary under fixed budget (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
11	Hierarchical pooling of confusion matrices across related subgroups may relax the per-subgroup budget requirement; we leave this extension to future work.
12	
13	Assumption~(A1) (conditional independence of misclassification and potential outcomes) is not empirically testable.
14	When LLM accuracy correlates with outcome magnitude---e.g., extreme sentiment is both easier to classify and associated with larger treatment effects---Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} acquires an $O(\gamma)$ perturbation (Section~\ref{sec:theory}).
15	Sensitivity simulation (Appendix~\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}) shows that EC-HTE maintains near-nominal coverage ($\geq$93.5\%) under outcome-dependent misclassification up to $\gamma = 0.2$, with bias increasing only 13.7\%; developing a formal closed-form bound for the $O(\gamma)$ perturbation remains a natural extension~\cite{lash2009applying,dorn2022sharp}.
16	
17	Oracle experiments confirm CausalForest plug-in SE is well-calibrated (94--96\% coverage with true $Z$ labels); EC-HTE plug-in SE achieves 93.8\% aggregate coverage under standard hyperparameters ($n_{\text{estimators}}{=}200$), with residual under-coverage concentrated in high-error subgroups due to asymmetric $M^{-1}$ SE propagation.
18	A full bootstrap procedure ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) recovers $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$.
19	For the DIM estimator, plug-in SE achieves $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets.
20	
21	The diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) achieves AUC $= 0.86$ under synthetic symmetric errors but degrades to $0.63$ on real LLM confusion matrices (pooled across 16 model--dataset combinations; Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
22	For $K{=}2$, the diagnostic anti-predicts because $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ forces score differentiation onto $1/\pi_s$ alone, which inversely correlates with actual harm; for binary $Z$, the asymmetric $B_s$-based formulation (Remark~2) is algebraically equivalent and offers no improvement.
23	Performance is strongest for $K{\geq}4$ with moderate asymmetry (AUC $= 0.66$; Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}).
24	The diagnostic remains a theoretically grounded criterion---the bias identity's product structure ensures it correctly identifies the \emph{direction} of bias amplification---but should be paired with $R^2$ validation of the bias identity rather than used as a standalone screening rule.
25	
26	All main experiments use symmetric error rates and additive CATE injection ($Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(Z)$).
27	The bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) generalizes to asymmetric confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}, $R^2 = 0.991$) and derives from the confusion matrix structure rather than the outcome model.
28	While our main experiments use additive CATE injection, a supplementary experiment with multiplicative effects ($Y(1) = Y(0) \times \exp(\tau(Z))$) yields comparable bias reduction (52\%) and nominal coverage (0.955; Appendix~\ref{app:rlearner}), confirming robustness to the functional form of treatment effects.
29	EC-HTE further requires discrete, pre-defined subgroups; subgroup definitions should be pre-specified based on domain knowledge, as data-driven subgroup discovery risks overfitting the confusion matrix structure to sample-specific noise. Continuous effect modifiers or latent subgroup discovery settings require different approaches, and intersectional subgroups with many levels may exceed the $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ budget threshold.
30	Our experiments define subgroups by text features (hashtag presence, text length); demographic subgroups---where prior work documents the most concerning disparities \citep{ashwin2025bias}---require sensitive data access beyond the scope of this study.
31	EC-HTE's correction mechanism is agnostic to subgroup definition: it corrects any per-subgroup confusion-matrix heterogeneity, whether defined by text features, demographics, or other covariates.
32	Ground-truth subgroup CATEs are unavailable in public datasets; classic causal inference benchmarks (e.g., LaLonde, IHDP) lack the LLM annotation step that creates the measurement error our method corrects, precluding direct application. We use synthetic CATE injection on real text features and real LLM annotations.
33	We leave full real-data validation---on a dataset combining RCT design, ground-truth CATEs, and LLM annotations---to future work as suitable public benchmarks become available.
34	Code and data generation scripts will be released upon acceptance.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

EC-HTE requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
For $K{=}2$, EC-HTE remains effective even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$ (Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}); for $K{=}4$, $P(Z{=}1) \geq 0.3$ is needed to approach breakeven with global correction at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$.
Even above this threshold, stratification incurs a variance cost: at $K{=}4$, extreme heterogeneity, and $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$, CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
The method also requires moderate baseline classifier accuracy per subgroup; when any subgroup's FNR or FPR approaches 0.5, the confusion matrix row approaches a uniform distribution and inversion amplifies noise (Appendix~\ref{app:semireal}), as confirmed independently in the hate speech case study (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
These failure modes interact: high per-subgroup error-rate variance combined with low minority prevalence $P(Z{=}1)$ jointly reduces effective per-subgroup expert labels for the positive class, compounding both sources of estimation error.
Additionally, our main semi-synthetic experiments use constant treatment effects across subgroups; a supplementary heterogeneous-$\tau$ DGP (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}) shows that EC-HTE achieves targeted bias and RMSE improvement in subgroups with large $\Delta\tau$, though aggregate RMSE remains comparable to global correction.
At $K{=}8$ with $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ (${\approx}31$ labels/subgroup), EC-HTE maintains nominal coverage (95.6\%) but RMSE exceeds global correction, establishing $K{=}8$ as a scalability boundary under fixed budget (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
Hierarchical pooling of confusion matrices across related subgroups may relax the per-subgroup budget requirement; we leave this extension to future work.

Assumption~(A1) (conditional independence of misclassification and potential outcomes) is not empirically testable.
When LLM accuracy correlates with outcome magnitude---e.g., extreme sentiment is both easier to classify and associated with larger treatment effects---Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} acquires an $O(\gamma)$ perturbation (Section~\ref{sec:theory}).
Sensitivity simulation (Appendix~\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}) shows that EC-HTE maintains near-nominal coverage ($\geq$93.5\%) under outcome-dependent misclassification up to $\gamma = 0.2$, with bias increasing only 13.7\%; developing a formal closed-form bound for the $O(\gamma)$ perturbation remains a natural extension~\cite{lash2009applying,dorn2022sharp}.

Oracle experiments confirm CausalForest plug-in SE is well-calibrated (94--96\% coverage with true $Z$ labels); EC-HTE plug-in SE achieves 93.8\% aggregate coverage under standard hyperparameters ($n_{\text{estimators}}{=}200$), with residual under-coverage concentrated in high-error subgroups due to asymmetric $M^{-1}$ SE propagation.
A full bootstrap procedure ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) recovers $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$.
For the DIM estimator, plug-in SE achieves $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets.

The diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) achieves AUC $= 0.86$ under synthetic symmetric errors but degrades to $0.63$ on real LLM confusion matrices (pooled across 16 model--dataset combinations; Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
For $K{=}2$, the diagnostic anti-predicts because $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ forces score differentiation onto $1/\pi_s$ alone, which inversely correlates with actual harm; for binary $Z$, the asymmetric $B_s$-based formulation (Remark~2) is algebraically equivalent and offers no improvement.
Performance is strongest for $K{\geq}4$ with moderate asymmetry (AUC $= 0.66$; Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}).
The diagnostic remains a theoretically grounded criterion---the bias identity's product structure ensures it correctly identifies the \emph{direction} of bias amplification---but should be paired with $R^2$ validation of the bias identity rather than used as a standalone screening rule.

All main experiments use symmetric error rates and additive CATE injection ($Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(Z)$).
The bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) generalizes to asymmetric confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}, $R^2 = 0.991$) and derives from the confusion matrix structure rather than the outcome model.
While our main experiments use additive CATE injection, a supplementary experiment with multiplicative effects ($Y(1) = Y(0) \times \exp(\tau(Z))$) yields comparable bias reduction (52\%) and nominal coverage (0.955; Appendix~\ref{app:rlearner}), confirming robustness to the functional form of treatment effects.
EC-HTE further requires discrete, pre-defined subgroups; subgroup definitions should be pre-specified based on domain knowledge, as data-driven subgroup discovery risks overfitting the confusion matrix structure to sample-specific noise. Continuous effect modifiers or latent subgroup discovery settings require different approaches, and intersectional subgroups with many levels may exceed the $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ budget threshold.
Our experiments define subgroups by text features (hashtag presence, text length); demographic subgroups---where prior work documents the most concerning disparities \citep{ashwin2025bias}---require sensitive data access beyond the scope of this study.
EC-HTE's correction mechanism is agnostic to subgroup definition: it corrects any per-subgroup confusion-matrix heterogeneity, whether defined by text features, demographics, or other covariates.
Ground-truth subgroup CATEs are unavailable in public datasets; classic causal inference benchmarks (e.g., LaLonde, IHDP) lack the LLM annotation step that creates the measurement error our method corrects, precluding direct application. We use synthetic CATE injection on real text features and real LLM annotations.
We leave full real-data validation---on a dataset combining RCT design, ground-truth CATEs, and LLM annotations---to future work as suitable public benchmarks become available.
Code and data generation scripts will be released upon acceptance.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Proxy classifiers---including LLMs now widely used to replace human coders---exhibit misclassification rates that vary substantially across subgroups, yet standard practice corrects annotation error using a single pooled confusion matrix.
3	We show that this global correction introduces structured bias into subgroup-level treatment effect estimates; in our LLM annotation experiments, global correction worsens bias in 50\% of configurations.
4	We derive a bias identity showing that this correction-induced bias factors into each subgroup's deviation from the pooled error rate times the treatment effect heterogeneity.
5	The identity yields a diagnostic that flags harmful correction using only per-subgroup error rates, without estimating treatment effects: on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity, the diagnostic achieves perfect separation (AUC $= 1.0$); the lower aggregate AUC on real LLM confusion matrices is driven by subgroups where correction is unnecessary.
6	We provide EC-HTE, the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity via hierarchical Bayes, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ by 7.4$\times$ under extreme heterogeneity with nominal coverage ($\geq$0.90); validated across synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments with multiple LLMs, the advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget.
7	\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
Proxy classifiers---including LLMs now widely used to replace human coders---exhibit misclassification rates that vary substantially across subgroups, yet standard practice corrects annotation error using a single pooled confusion matrix.
We show that this global correction introduces structured bias into subgroup-level treatment effect estimates; in our LLM annotation experiments, global correction worsens bias in 50\% of configurations.
We derive a bias identity showing that this correction-induced bias factors into each subgroup's deviation from the pooled error rate times the treatment effect heterogeneity.
The identity yields a diagnostic that flags harmful correction using only per-subgroup error rates, without estimating treatment effects: on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity, the diagnostic achieves perfect separation (AUC $= 1.0$); the lower aggregate AUC on real LLM confusion matrices is driven by subgroups where correction is unnecessary.
We provide EC-HTE, the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity via hierarchical Bayes, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ by 7.4$\times$ under extreme heterogeneity with nominal coverage ($\geq$0.90); validated across synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments with multiple LLMs, the advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:intro}
3	
4	Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
5	Yet these annotations are not uniformly accurate.
6	\citet{ashwin2025bias} document that LLM misclassification rates vary by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level.
7	In a pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% binary accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).
8	When such annotations serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, subgroup-specific errors propagate directly into conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
9	The resulting bias is not random noise that averages out; it is structured by the same demographic axes that define the research question.
10	Standard correction procedures\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.}, which estimate a single confusion matrix and apply its inverse uniformly, cannot account for this heterogeneity.
11	
12	We formalize this problem and derive a bias identity for the correction-induced error.
13	When a pooled confusion matrix is applied to correct subgroup CATEs, it misattributes error across subgroups with an exact product form: the bias in subgroup $s$ equals $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, where $\delta_s$ is the deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau$ is the CATE heterogeneity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
14	This is not a bound but an exact population-level identity, verified empirically with $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $R^2 = 0.974$ ($K{=}4$) on synthetic grids, and $R^2 = 0.975$ across 11 real LLM confusion matrices spanning open-source and proprietary model families.
15	A direct consequence is that global correction can be worse than no correction at all: global correction worsens CATE bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520) across our parameter grid---concentrated in regimes where $\Delta\pi > 0.10$ and per-subgroup expert samples exceed 25---with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest).
16	The bias identity also yields a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction will increase bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic})---independently useful even without adopting EC-HTE, since practitioners can flag harmful correction from a pilot sample before estimating any treatment effects.
17	Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation.
18	EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit---the expected bias-variance tradeoff of any subgroup-stratified correction (Figure~\ref{fig:bias_mechanism}).
19	
20	Subgroup CATEs inform resource allocation---e.g., whether a policy reduces toxicity more in long-form versus short-form posts---and biased estimates can reverse the sign of apparent heterogeneity, directing resources away from communities that benefit most.
21	The failure mode is subtle: correcting for annotation noise using a pooled confusion matrix may introduce more bias than doing nothing, precisely in the low-error subgroups where labels were most trustworthy.
22	
23	Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---address population-level or outcome-side measurement error but assume homogeneous prediction error across subgroups; none corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function (Section~\ref{sec:related}).
24	
25	\begin{figure}[t]
26	\centering
27	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_bias_mechanism.pdf}
28	\caption{Bias mechanism under global vs.\ subgroup-stratified correction. Global correction applies the pooled error rate $\bar{\pi}$ uniformly, over-correcting low-error subgroups (introducing bias where none existed) and under-correcting high-error subgroups. EC-HTE matches each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification rate.}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
Yet these annotations are not uniformly accurate.
\citet{ashwin2025bias} document that LLM misclassification rates vary by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level.
In a pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% binary accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).
When such annotations serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, subgroup-specific errors propagate directly into conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
The resulting bias is not random noise that averages out; it is structured by the same demographic axes that define the research question.
Standard correction procedures\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.}, which estimate a single confusion matrix and apply its inverse uniformly, cannot account for this heterogeneity.

We formalize this problem and derive a bias identity for the correction-induced error.
When a pooled confusion matrix is applied to correct subgroup CATEs, it misattributes error across subgroups with an exact product form: the bias in subgroup $s$ equals $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, where $\delta_s$ is the deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau$ is the CATE heterogeneity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
This is not a bound but an exact population-level identity, verified empirically with $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $R^2 = 0.974$ ($K{=}4$) on synthetic grids, and $R^2 = 0.975$ across 11 real LLM confusion matrices spanning open-source and proprietary model families.
A direct consequence is that global correction can be worse than no correction at all: global correction worsens CATE bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520) across our parameter grid---concentrated in regimes where $\Delta\pi > 0.10$ and per-subgroup expert samples exceed 25---with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest).
The bias identity also yields a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction will increase bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic})---independently useful even without adopting EC-HTE, since practitioners can flag harmful correction from a pilot sample before estimating any treatment effects.
Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit---the expected bias-variance tradeoff of any subgroup-stratified correction (Figure~\ref{fig:bias_mechanism}).

Subgroup CATEs inform resource allocation---e.g., whether a policy reduces toxicity more in long-form versus short-form posts---and biased estimates can reverse the sign of apparent heterogeneity, directing resources away from communities that benefit most.
The failure mode is subtle: correcting for annotation noise using a pooled confusion matrix may introduce more bias than doing nothing, precisely in the low-error subgroups where labels were most trustworthy.

Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---address population-level or outcome-side measurement error but assume homogeneous prediction error across subgroups; none corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_bias_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{Bias mechanism under global vs.\ subgroup-stratified correction. Global correction applies the pooled error rate $\bar{\pi}$ uniformly, over-correcting low-error subgroups (introducing bias where none existed) and under-correcting high-error subgroups. EC-HTE matches each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification rate.}
\label{fig:bias_mechanism}
\end{figure}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): global confusion-matrix correction introduces subgroup CATE bias proportional to each subgroup's misclassification deviation times the treatment effect heterogeneity---a bias decomposition with independent diagnostic value, verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 11 real LLM confusion matrices (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
    \item A $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) derived from the identity: a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity---independently actionable without EC-HTE (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE, the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the bias structure via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation, compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error; we characterize applicability conditions and crossover budgets (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}; Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}
While we develop the theory and experiments for LLM annotation---the leading practical case---the bias identity applies whenever any proxy classifier with subgroup-varying error rates is used to construct effect modifiers for causal inference.

6	The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
7	
8	\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}
9	
10	We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
11	For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
12	Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
13	This partial pooling---a James-Stein shrinkage effect---borrows strength across subgroups, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.
14	
15	Posterior inference uses Gibbs sampling (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
16	HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
17	The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
18	At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
19	Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.
20	
21	\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}
22	
23	Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
24	\begin{equation}
25	\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
26	\end{equation}
27	where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
28	This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
29	In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
30	We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
31	This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; a separate empirical diagnostic ($\kappa \leq 1.25$, Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}) identifies the tighter regime where stratified correction reliably outperforms global.
32	
33	The contrast with global correction is direct.
34	Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
35	Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
36	
37	\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}
38	
39	For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
40	The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
41	To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
42	\begin{equation}
43	\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
44	\end{equation}
45	This is a plug-in approach: the standard errors reflect outcome variance conditional on $\hat{C}_s$ but do not propagate uncertainty from the confusion matrix estimation itself.
46	At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$, the plug-in approximation is reasonable because confusion matrix estimation variance is small relative to outcome variance.
47	Below this threshold, the standard errors may understate total uncertainty.
48	A full bootstrap procedure (re-estimating both the confusion matrix and the downstream estimator per replicate, $B{=}100$) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even the plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% coverage at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$, confirming the method's reliability across the practical range (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
49	
50	\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
51	Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
52	This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
53	A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
54	
55	\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
56	EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
57	PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
58	The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
59	Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
60	Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).

\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
\label{sec:method}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).

\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}

We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
This partial pooling---a James-Stein shrinkage effect---borrows strength across subgroups, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.

Posterior inference uses Gibbs sampling (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.

\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}

Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; a separate empirical diagnostic ($\kappa \leq 1.25$, Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}) identifies the tighter regime where stratified correction reliably outperforms global.

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}

For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
\begin{equation}
\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
\end{equation}
This is a plug-in approach: the standard errors reflect outcome variance conditional on $\hat{C}_s$ but do not propagate uncertainty from the confusion matrix estimation itself.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$, the plug-in approximation is reasonable because confusion matrix estimation variance is small relative to outcome variance.
Below this threshold, the standard errors may understate total uncertainty.
A full bootstrap procedure (re-estimating both the confusion matrix and the downstream estimator per replicate, $B{=}100$) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even the plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% coverage at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$, confirming the method's reliability across the practical range (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).

\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
5	Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.
6	
7	Three distinctions separate our contribution from prior measurement error analyses.
8	First, we study effect modifier misclassification---the mismeasured variable defines the CATE function itself---rather than regressor~\cite{frazis2003estimating,carroll2006measurement} or confounder~\cite{ogburn2012nondifferential,greenland1980effect} error, where attenuation is the primary concern.
9	Second, Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} derives a bias identity for correction-induced bias---bias created by the debiasing procedure---rather than bounding the attenuation from misclassification itself.
10	Concretely, \citet{frazis2003estimating} derive scalar attenuation for the uncorrected estimator under homogeneous misclassification; Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} characterizes a structurally distinct quantity---correction-induced bias that is subgroup-specific, potentially sign-reversing, and absent from the uncorrected estimator.
11	The homogeneous-error setting ($K{=}1$, $\delta_s{=}0$) is a degenerate case recovering classical attenuation~\cite{blackwell2017unified}; empirically, F-L correction produces higher bias under heterogeneous misclassification, while EC-HTE achieves near-oracle performance (Appendix~\ref{app:fl_comparison}).
12	Third, the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure arises only under heterogeneous error rates; all homogeneous-error analyses~\cite{battistin2014treatment,fong2021machine} miss this interaction entirely.
13	In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
14	Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.
15	
16	\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
17	Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml,semenova2021debiased}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
18	EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
19	The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
20	For broader perspectives on causal inference with text data, see \citet{feder2022causal} and \citet{keith2020text}; \citet{wang2020methods} study inference correction when outcomes are ML-predicted, a related but distinct problem from effect modifier misclassification.
21	LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups; \citet{cheng2024err} demonstrate that prompt optimization can reduce such error, a complementary preprocessing step.
22	This subgroup-varying error distorts the very contrasts that define the research question; prior work documents the pattern without correcting downstream causal estimands.
23	Concurrent work identifies variance-side LLM measurement error~\cite{messing2026hidden}; \citet{camuffo2025variance} characterize five variance sources in LLM annotation, complementary to our bias-side analysis.
24	Temperature or Platt scaling~\cite{guo2017calibration} reduces per-subgroup $\pi_s$ but does not eliminate heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$; EC-HTE corrects the residual $\delta_s$-driven bias that persists post-calibration (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration} empirically confirms this complementarity).
25	
26	\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
27	PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
28	In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
29	EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
30	\citet{audinet2025benchmarking} benchmark DSL and PPI debiasing for LLM-based parameter estimation, documenting bias-variance tradeoffs analogous to our findings; their analysis targets population-level parameters rather than subgroup-conditional estimands, leaving the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ interaction we formalize unaddressed.
31	\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
32	None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
33	\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification via instrumental variables or partial identification; \citet{ura2015heterogeneous} extends this to HTE with mismeasured treatment via IV.
34	Our problem is structurally distinct: the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting correction through confusion matrices.
35	Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
36	Our validation combines synthetic DGPs, semi-synthetic experiments, and real LLM confusion matrices, consistent with PPI and DSL evaluation methodology; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm} validates both $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity and the bias identity itself ($R^2 = 0.975$) across 11 model--dataset combinations.
37

Concretely, \citet{frazis2003estimating} derive scalar attenuation for the uncorrected estimator under homogeneous misclassification; Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} characterizes a structurally distinct quantity---correction-induced bias that is subgroup-specific, potentially sign-reversing, and absent from the uncorrected estimator.

Third, the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ product structure arises only under heterogeneous error rates; all homogeneous-error analyses~\cite{battistin2014treatment,fong2021machine} miss this interaction entirely.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml,semenova2021debiased}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
For broader perspectives on causal inference with text data, see \citet{feder2022causal} and \citet{keith2020text}; \citet{wang2020methods} study inference correction when outcomes are ML-predicted, a related but distinct problem from effect modifier misclassification.
LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups; \citet{cheng2024err} demonstrate that prompt optimization can reduce such error, a complementary preprocessing step.
This subgroup-varying error distorts the very contrasts that define the research question; prior work documents the pattern without correcting downstream causal estimands.
Concurrent work identifies variance-side LLM measurement error~\cite{messing2026hidden}; \citet{camuffo2025variance} characterize five variance sources in LLM annotation, complementary to our bias-side analysis.
Temperature or Platt scaling~\cite{guo2017calibration} reduces per-subgroup $\pi_s$ but does not eliminate heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$; EC-HTE corrects the residual $\delta_s$-driven bias that persists post-calibration (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration} empirically confirms this complementarity).

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
In our setting---binary effect modifier with known subgroup structure, a special case of the broader problems DSL addresses---DSL's measurement error correction reduces, under the confusion-matrix parameterization we adopt, to confusion matrix inversion: pooled DSL is equivalent to our Global baseline, and per-subgroup DSL to Stratified MLE (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}; Appendix~\ref{app:ppi_comparison}).
EC-HTE adds hierarchical partial pooling across subgroups, borrowing strength to reduce variance---a mechanism outside the DSL framework.
\citet{audinet2025benchmarking} benchmark DSL and PPI debiasing for LLM-based parameter estimation, documenting bias-variance tradeoffs analogous to our findings; their analysis targets population-level parameters rather than subgroup-conditional estimands, leaving the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ interaction we formalize unaddressed.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification via instrumental variables or partial identification; \citet{ura2015heterogeneous} extends this to HTE with mismeasured treatment via IV.
Our problem is structurally distinct: the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting correction through confusion matrices.
Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.
Our validation combines synthetic DGPs, semi-synthetic experiments, and real LLM confusion matrices, consistent with PPI and DSL evaluation methodology; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm} validates both $\Delta\pi$ heterogeneity and the bias identity itself ($R^2 = 0.975$) across 11 model--dataset combinations.

Under \textnormal{(A1)--(A5)}, global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator ($|\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{global}}| > |\mathrm{bias}_{\mathrm{naive}}|$) in subgroup $s$ if and only if
\begin{equation}
\frac{|\delta_s|}{(1 - 2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s} > 1.
\label{eq:hurts_condition}
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

Equation~\eqref{eq:hurts_condition} partitions subgroups into two regimes.
For high-error subgroups ($\pi_s > \bar{\pi}$), the condition reduces to $\pi_s > 0.5$, excluded by~(A4).
For low-error subgroups ($\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$), it holds whenever $\pi_s < \bar{\pi} / (2(1 - \bar{\pi}))$---easily satisfied: when $\bar{\pi} = 0.15$, any subgroup with $\pi_s < 0.088$ is harmed.
The mechanism is over-correction: global inversion applies a correction calibrated for the average error rate, so low-error subgroups are overcorrected (the correction overshoots and reverses bias sign) while high-error subgroups are under-corrected.
For subgroups with near-zero misclassification ($\pi_s \approx 0$), the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet global correction creates substantial bias---debiasing can be worse than doing nothing.

In our experiments (Section~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}), global correction increases bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations across our parameter grid (260 of 520, excluding cases where $\Delta\pi{=}0$).
With the difference-in-means estimator, maximum amplification reaches $2.86\times$ for $K{=}2$ and $2.41\times$ for $K{=}4$; the mechanism operates across estimator types, with nonlinear estimators amplifying the effect further (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}).
Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification across the full $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ parameter grid.

\section{MCMC Convergence Diagnostics}
\label{app:mcmc}

Table~\ref{tab:mcmc} reports convergence diagnostics for the hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimator across all experimental configurations.
All runs use 4 chains with 4000 iterations (2000 warmup).
Main experiments (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}) use a Dirichlet prior centered on $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ with concentration $\alpha_0$ estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood).
Appendix robustness experiments use a fixed Dirichlet prior ($\alpha{=}3$); since fixed-$\alpha$ partial pooling is weakly dominated by the adaptive variant, these results are conservative.
This budget is sufficient for the $2{\times}2$ Dirichlet-Multinomial posterior; all runs achieve $\hat{R} < 1.0034$ and ESS $> 1618$, confirming convergence with substantial margin.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Diagnostic & Threshold & Achieved \\

\begin{abstract}
Proxy classifiers---including LLMs now widely used to replace human coders---exhibit misclassification rates that vary substantially across subgroups, yet standard practice corrects annotation error using a single pooled confusion matrix.
We show that this global correction introduces structured bias into subgroup-level treatment effect estimates; in our LLM annotation experiments, global correction worsens bias in 50\% of configurations.
We derive a bias identity showing that this correction-induced bias factors into each subgroup's deviation from the pooled error rate times the treatment effect heterogeneity.
The identity yields a diagnostic that flags harmful correction using only per-subgroup error rates, without estimating treatment effects: on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity, the diagnostic achieves perfect separation (AUC $= 1.0$); the lower aggregate AUC on real LLM confusion matrices is driven by subgroups where correction is unnecessary.
We provide EC-HTE, the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity via hierarchical Bayes, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ by 7.4$\times$ under extreme heterogeneity with nominal coverage ($\geq$0.90); validated across synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments with multiple LLMs, the advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget.
\end{abstract}

We show that this global correction introduces structured bias into subgroup-level treatment effect estimates; in our LLM annotation experiments, global correction worsens bias in 50\% of configurations.
We derive a bias identity showing that this correction-induced bias factors into each subgroup's deviation from the pooled error rate times the treatment effect heterogeneity.
The identity yields a diagnostic that flags harmful correction using only per-subgroup error rates, without estimating treatment effects: on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity, the diagnostic achieves perfect separation (AUC $= 1.0$); the lower aggregate AUC on real LLM confusion matrices is driven by subgroups where correction is unnecessary.
We provide EC-HTE, the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity via hierarchical Bayes, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ by 7.4$\times$ under extreme heterogeneity with nominal coverage ($\geq$0.90); validated across synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments with multiple LLMs, the advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
Yet these annotations are not uniformly accurate.
\citet{ashwin2025bias} document that LLM misclassification rates vary by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level.
In a pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% binary accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).
When such annotations serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, subgroup-specific errors propagate directly into conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
The resulting bias is not random noise that averages out; it is structured by the same demographic axes that define the research question.
Standard correction procedures\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.}, which estimate a single confusion matrix and apply its inverse uniformly, cannot account for this heterogeneity.

We formalize this problem and derive a bias identity for the correction-induced error.
When a pooled confusion matrix is applied to correct subgroup CATEs, it misattributes error across subgroups with an exact product form: the bias in subgroup $s$ equals $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, where $\delta_s$ is the deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau$ is the CATE heterogeneity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
This is not a bound but an exact population-level identity, verified empirically with $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $R^2 = 0.974$ ($K{=}4$) on synthetic grids, and $R^2 = 0.975$ across 11 real LLM confusion matrices spanning open-source and proprietary model families.
A direct consequence is that global correction can be worse than no correction at all: global correction worsens CATE bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520) across our parameter grid---concentrated in regimes where $\Delta\pi > 0.10$ and per-subgroup expert samples exceed 25---with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest).
The bias identity also yields a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction will increase bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic})---independently useful even without adopting EC-HTE, since practitioners can flag harmful correction from a pilot sample before estimating any treatment effects.
Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit---the expected bias-variance tradeoff of any subgroup-stratified correction (Figure~\ref{fig:bias_mechanism}).

Subgroup CATEs inform resource allocation---e.g., whether a policy reduces toxicity more in long-form versus short-form posts---and biased estimates can reverse the sign of apparent heterogeneity, directing resources away from communities that benefit most.
The failure mode is subtle: correcting for annotation noise using a pooled confusion matrix may introduce more bias than doing nothing, precisely in the low-error subgroups where labels were most trustworthy.

Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---address population-level or outcome-side measurement error but assume homogeneous prediction error across subgroups; none corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_bias_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{Bias mechanism under global vs.\ subgroup-stratified correction. Global correction applies the pooled error rate $\bar{\pi}$ uniformly, over-correcting low-error subgroups (introducing bias where none existed) and under-correcting high-error subgroups. EC-HTE matches each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification rate.}
\label{fig:bias_mechanism}
\end{figure}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): global confusion-matrix correction introduces subgroup CATE bias proportional to each subgroup's misclassification deviation times the treatment effect heterogeneity---a bias decomposition with independent diagnostic value, verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 11 real LLM confusion matrices (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
    \item A $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) derived from the identity: a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity---independently actionable without EC-HTE (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE, the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the bias structure via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation, compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error; we characterize applicability conditions and crossover budgets (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}; Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}
While we develop the theory and experiments for LLM annotation---the leading practical case---the bias identity applies whenever any proxy classifier with subgroup-varying error rates is used to construct effect modifiers for causal inference.

\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
\label{sec:method}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).

\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}

We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
This partial pooling---a James-Stein shrinkage effect---borrows strength across subgroups, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.

Posterior inference uses Gibbs sampling (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.

\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}

Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; a separate empirical diagnostic ($\kappa \leq 1.25$, Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}) identifies the tighter regime where stratified correction reliably outperforms global.

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}

For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
\begin{equation}
\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
\end{equation}
This is a plug-in approach: the standard errors reflect outcome variance conditional on $\hat{C}_s$ but do not propagate uncertainty from the confusion matrix estimation itself.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$, the plug-in approximation is reasonable because confusion matrix estimation variance is small relative to outcome variance.
Below this threshold, the standard errors may understate total uncertainty.
A full bootstrap procedure (re-estimating both the confusion matrix and the downstream estimator per replicate, $B{=}100$) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even the plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% coverage at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$, confirming the method's reliability across the practical range (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).

\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).

\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
\label{sec:method}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).

\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}

We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
This partial pooling---a James-Stein shrinkage effect---borrows strength across subgroups, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.
We apply hierarchical Bayesian partial pooling---well-established in small-area estimation---to confusion matrix estimation, a setting where subgroup-specific misclassification rates must be estimated from limited expert labels.

Posterior inference uses Gibbs sampling (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.

\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}

Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; a separate empirical diagnostic ($\kappa \leq 1.25$, Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}) identifies the tighter regime where stratified correction reliably outperforms global.

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}

For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
\begin{equation}
\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
\end{equation}
This is a plug-in approach: the standard errors reflect outcome variance conditional on $\hat{C}_s$ but do not propagate uncertainty from the confusion matrix estimation itself.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$, the plug-in approximation is reasonable because confusion matrix estimation variance is small relative to outcome variance.
Below this threshold, the standard errors may understate total uncertainty.
A full bootstrap procedure (re-estimating both the confusion matrix and the downstream estimator per replicate, $B{=}100$) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even the plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% coverage at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$, confirming the method's reliability across the practical range (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).

\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).
